items.can_do: Can use a list of adjectives in ellipted clauses before and after a noun, to give focus. ► focus
Can combine more complex, lengthy strings of adjectives, joining the last two adjectives with 'and'.
Can use 'no' / 'not any' with comparative adjectives to limit the scale of comparison. ► comparative clauses
Can use 'not that much' to modify comparative adjectives to a small degree. ► comparative clauses
Can use adjectives in 'as … as' and 'so … that' in comparative structures. ► comparative clauses
Can use an increasing range of adjectives before a noun to express intensity.
Can use 'the slightest', 'the faintest' with a specific range of nouns to express the least amount possible, most frequently following a negative verb form.

items.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
items.can_do: Can use adverbs mid clause, to distance the writer from what they are saying.
Can use adverbs in mid position, to distance the writer from what they are saying.
Can use 'hardly' in front position followed by an inverted subject and verb, to give focus.
Can form adverb phrases with modifiers before, and complements after, adverbs.
Can use 'so' + adjective + 'as' + 'to'-infinitive clause, usually in formal contexts.
Can use 'as if' + non-finite clause to introduce a second clause as a comparison.
Can combine a negative clause with an inverted clause with 'nor', to give focus.

items.guideword: FORM/USE: 'LET' + THIRD PERSON PRONOUN, DEVOLVING RESPONSIBILITY
items.can_do: Can use an imperative clause with 'let' + 'him/her/them' + base form of a main verb, to devolve responsibility.
Can use you with an imperative form to make an instruction stronger.
Can use 'How' + clause.
Can use 'How' + adverb + clause.
Can use 'Were' + pronoun + 'to' infinitive to introduce a condition, in formal contexts.
Can use non-finite clauses after subordinating conjunctions '(although, though)', to express contrast.

items.guideword: FORM/USE: INVERTED PAST PERFECT, IMAGINED PAST
items.can_do: Can use past perfect +  inverted subject, and a modal verb + 'have' + '-ed' in the main clause  to talk about imagined situations in the past.

items.guideword: USE: INVERTED 'SHOULD', FUTURE, POSSIBLE OUTCOME, FORMAL, POLITE
items.can_do: Can use inverted 'should', + 'would' in the main clause to talk about possible future outcomes, in polite or formal contexts.
Can use 'Were it not for' + noun phrase to introduce conditions in formal contexts. ► past simple
Can use 'were' with an inverted subject + 'to' infinitive, to introduce conditions in formal contexts. ► past simple
Can use conditional subordinate clauses with a range of conjunctions ('so long as', 'on condition that', 'in the event that') with past, present or future reference.|

items.guideword: FORM/USE: 'IF IT WERE NOT FOR', FORMAL
items.can_do: Can use 'If it weren’t / were not for' + noun phrase to introduce conditions in formal contexts. ► past simple
Can use 'If it were' + 'to-' infinitive to introduce conditions in formal contexts.
Can use 'whether or not' to introduce conditions in formal contexts.
Can use 'Neither' or 'Nor' + inverted auxiliary or 'be' + subject to add to a previous related negative clause, to focus on an additional negative factor.
Can use 'And yet' to combine sentences to introduce a contrast, often unexpected, sometimes in a formal context.
Can use 'in that' as a subordinating conjunction, to give greater in-depth explanation, often in formal contexts.
Can use 'this' with nouns and noun phrases in a narrative to create a sense of immediacy.
Can use 'this' + noun + 'of' + possessive pronoun to highlight something, often in a positive way.
Can use 'that' and 'those' to convey emotional distance, often to express disapproval.

items.guideword: FORM: SINGULAR NOUN ENDING IN 'S' + APOSTROPHE
items.can_do: Can use an apostrophe after singular nouns ending in 's', to indicate possession.
Can use two possessive ''s' constructions in the same noun phrase.
Can use ''s' without a following noun when the noun has already been mentioned or is obvious in the context.

items.guideword: FORM/USE: 'MANY A' WITH SINGULAR NOUNS, FOR FOCUS
items.can_do: Can use 'many a' or 'many an' + singular noun for emphasis and focus.
Can use 'Not a' + noun with a passive verb or inverted auxiliary and subject for focus.
Can use 'The' + premodifier + 'thing, fact, point, problem or reason' + 'is (that)' for focus.
Can use 'How', 'Why', or 'Where' cleft clauses as subject, for focus
Can use 'It' + 'be' + noun + 'that' clause for focus.
Can use more than one fixed expression in the front position for added focus.
Can use the simple past form of 'be' + 'due to' to talk about scheduled events in the future from a point in the past.
Can use the future perfect continuous to make assumptions about the present.
Can use the question form of the future perfect simple.
Can use 'shall' to talk about long-term intentions.
Can use 'shall' to make predictions, usually in formal contexts.
Can use 'be' + 'going to' with a wide range of adverbs before the main verb.
Can use the present simple with 'only when' (followed by 'will' and inverted subject) to refer to the future.
Can use 'how can' to reflect, through rhetorical questions.
Can use the negative form 'didn't dare' + infinitive without 'to' to talk about not being brave enough to do something.
Can use 'be' + 'not' + adjective + 'to' + infinitive.
Can use 'be' + adjective + 'not' + 'to' + infinitive for emphasis.
Can use present and past forms of 'have to' + '-ed' to talk about obligations in the past.
Can use a range of present and past forms of 'have (got) to' to talk about deductions and conclusions.  ► must  ► had to
Can use 'have to have' + '-ed'.

Can use 'may as well' to talk about what we think is the easiest or most logical course of action, often when we cannot see a better alternative or when it will not spoil the situation if you do that thing. ► might
Can use 'it may be' + '-ed' that as a hedging device when drawing conclusions and summarising, particularly in academic contexts.
Can use 'may' in a subordinate clause expressing concession with 'however', 'whatever', 'whoever' … + 'it or this may be or seem'.
Can use 'try as I might' for emphasis at the beginning of a sentence.
Can use 'might as well', mostly to talk about or suggest what we think is the easiest or most logical course of action, often when we cannot see a better alternative. ► 'may'
Can use ellipted 'must have' + '-ed' without a subject. ► ellipsis
Can use 'must not have been' (especially with 'easy').
Can use 'must' with a wide range of adverbs in the normal mid position after the modal verb. ► adverbs|
Can invert 'must' and the subject after negative phrases, e.g. 'not only', 'never', 'nor', to change the focus and give prominence/emphasis.
Can use the question form.
Can use the question form rhetorically in discussion, typically in formal contexts.
Can use 'oughtn't' (without 'to') + verb.
Can use 'ought' + subject + 'not to' + verb to form (rhetorical) questions, often in formal contexts.
Can use the negative form 'ought not to'.
Can use 'shall' in the main clause after an 'if-' clause  ► conditionals
Can use 'shall' to make predictions.
Can use 'as' + pronoun + 'used to' … to add background to a narrative, often to highlight something unusual.
Can use negative form 'used not to'
Can use 'will' to talk about general behaviour, often disapprovingly.
Can use a wide range of adverbs with 'would', including 'undoubtedly', 'possibly', 'normally', 'personally', 'eventually', 'obviously', 'significantly', 'inevitably'. ► adverbs
Can use adverbs expressing certainty as short responses.
Can use 'couldn’t have' + '-ed' to speculate about the past.
Can use 'not a' + noun, often with a following  passive structure, for emphasis.
Can use a negative imperative form with 'you' to give a warning or reprimand.
Can use 'Neither' or 'Nor' + with 'do' or 'be' + inverted subject to add to a previous related negative clause, to focus on an additional negative factor.
Can use 'in the least' after a negative form for emphasis.

items.guideword: FORM: COMPLEX NOUN PHRASES WITH 'LITTLE OR NO'  + NOUN
items.can_do: Can form complex noun phrases with 'little or no' + noun.
Can use passive non-finite '-ing' perfect forms in subordinate clauses to give explanatory background information.
Can use non-finite '-ing' perfect forms of the passive as the complement of prepositions.
Can use 'have' + object + infinitive without 'to' to talk about asking or causing someone to do something, often in formal contexts.
Can use the past continuous with 'always' or 'constantly' to talk about repeated events which are undesired or uncontrolled.
Can use the question form.

items.guideword: FORM: FIXED EXPRESSIONS 'HAD IT NOT BEEN FOR', 'IF IT HADN'T BEEN FOR'
items.can_do: Can use 'had it not been for' … and 'if it hadn’t been for' with a modal form for giving reasons.
Can use the negative form after 'if only' to express regret.
Can invert the subject and affirmative auxiliary verb with 'hardly … when' to talk about something that happened immediately before something else, in formal contexts.
Can invert the subject and affirmative auxiliary verb with 'not only … but' as a focusing device. ► focus ► inversion
Can use the present perfect simple to introduce news.
Can use the present continuous with verbs that are not usually used in this form to make statements and requests sound less direct.

items.guideword: FORM/USE: WITH ADVERBS OF INDEFINITE FREQUENCY
items.can_do: Can use the present continuous with a wide range of adverbs of indefinite frequency, often to talk about surprising or undesirable situations or events.
Can use 'that … of' + possessive pronouns to express an attitude about someone or something, often in humorous or sarcastic contexts.
Can use the possessive pronoun 'his', with singular and plural reference, in subject and object position, and complement positions after 'be' and after prepositions.
Can use the possessive pronoun 'theirs', with singular and plural reference, in subject position.
Can use the possessive pronoun 'hers' with singular reference, in subject position.
Can use the possessive pronouns 'hers', 'theirs' and 'his' after noun + 'of'.
Can use 'as for myself' as a discourse marker to introduce or focus on a personal opinion.
Can form a cleft construction beginning with 'it' to emphasise the subject of the main clause. ► clauses
Can use 'a lot' and 'much' as a subject pronouns. ► focus

items.guideword: FORM/USE: 'MANY ARE THE' + NOUN, FOR FOCUS
items.can_do: Can form complex noun phrases using an inverted form 'Many' + 'are' + noun phrase, followed by a relative clause, as a focusing device.  ► focus
Can use 'The one(s) that' + clause in subject position, for focus. ► focus
Can use 'each' (+ noun or pronoun) as subject followed by 'the other(s)' as object , to refer to two related things. ► pronouns: quantity
Can form alternative questions with two or more clauses and ellipsis in the second or third clause.
Can form negative questions with uncontracted 'not' to emphasise a point in an argument.

items.guideword: FORM: VERB + DIRECT OBJECT + PARTICLE + PREPOSITION + OBJECT
items.can_do: Can use a direct object with some prepositional verbs as well as an object of the preposition.
Can use 'would hate' + 'to' infinitive, for emphasis.
